name: Evidence Action India BOTEC
summary: Gives technical help to Indian state governments to run health programs such as iron supplementation. GiveWell's spreadsheet "Evidence Action India BOTEC", linked from its grant page. Every number is traced from the sheet's bottom line; calculated rows reproduce the sheet's own values.

Indian state annual government spending on IFA
Amount of government funds crowded in (% increase)
rows.explainer: We don't have any info. Assumed a 10% increase per year for a few years; I don't have any obvious benchmarks to work with here. I don't know if it's a similar model to deworming, where they could get more states to do this program that aren't currently doing it (in which case they could "crowd in" lots more funds) or if the program is already operating nationally and is fully funded (in which case it seems like potential for crowding in would be smaller). I don't think Evidence Action has a strong sense of the situation yet either and they said they expected most of their impact to be from coverage increases initially. That said, given the number of kids in India (~250 million), seems like it'd cost a lot more than the Indian government is currently spending to cover everyone with IFA supplementation for the year. Units of value per dollar given to GiveDirectly
rows.explainer: GiveWell reports this model's result in multiples of cash transfers. Multiplying by GiveWell's value of a dollar to GiveDirectly converts it into units of value per dollar, so it ranks against the other models. Older sheets used older moral weights; the multiple of cash is the comparable number across years.
